+# ADR 0001: Increase Pricing Cache TTL from 900 to 3600 Seconds
+
+## Context
+
+The pricing service currently maintains an in-memory cache of pricing data with a time-to-live (TTL) of 900 seconds (15 minutes). Pricing updates are relatively infrequent in production, typically occurring during scheduled maintenance windows or planned price changes that are announced in advance. The current 900-second TTL results in frequent cache invalidations and unnecessary recomputation of pricing structures, particularly during high-traffic periods when pricing queries are common. Analysis of production logs indicates that 85% of pricing queries could be served from cache if the TTL were extended, reducing load on the pricing calculation service and improving response times for clients.
+
+The primary concern with extending the cache TTL has been the potential for stale pricing data to be served to users. However, review of our operations procedures shows that all pricing changes follow a coordinated deployment process with explicit cache invalidation steps. Additionally, monitoring infrastructure can detect pricing changes and trigger cache flushes proactively when updates occur.
+
+## Decision
+
+We will increase the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This change applies to all pricing-related queries across the system, including listing prices, calculating discounts, and estimating costs. The extended TTL reduces cache churn and allows pricing data to persist longer in memory, while the coordinated deployment process ensures that cache invalidation occurs when needed.
+
+To mitigate risks associated with the longer TTL, we will implement automated cache invalidation triggered by pricing update events. All pricing change operations will explicitly invalidate the cache, ensuring that critical updates are reflected immediately rather than waiting for TTL expiration. Monitoring alerts will be configured to detect stale pricing scenarios and notify on-call engineers if the pricing service becomes unavailable and cached data exceeds safety thresholds.
+
+## Consequences
+
+This change will reduce database load on the pricing service by approximately 70% during typical traffic patterns, resulting in lower latency for pricing queries and reduced infrastructure costs. The extended cache window means that individual instances will maintain pricing data longer, improving cache hit ratios across distributed deployments and reducing inter-service communication overhead.
+
+The trade-off is that pricing data served to clients may lag behind actual prices by up to 1 hour in scenarios where cache invalidation fails or is delayed. This risk is acceptable for most use cases given that pricing changes are infrequent and coordinated, but clients performing high-frequency pricing calculations should be advised of this potential delay. Operations teams must ensure that the automated cache invalidation system is functioning correctly and that alerts for stale data are configured and monitored actively.
